translationRepairs: In the sixteenth year he joined Minister Tang Jinzhao on an investigative tour of Shaanxi and Sichuan to impeach Governor Yang Mingyang and provincial administration commissioner Li Yiwen; both cases went to strict review. When the inquiry into denunciations against Yang was reopened, Wen Qing himself was dismissed.

In the sixteenth year he joined Minister Tang Jinzhao on an investigative tour of Shaanxi and Sichuan to impeach Governor Yang Mingyang and provincial administration commissioner Li Yiwen; both cases went to strict review. When the inquiry into denunciations against Yang was reopened, Yang was stripped of office.
After 尋复按名颺被訐事, 褫其職 most naturally demotes Yang Mingyang; Wen Qing continues investigating in the next sentences, so the English wrongly making Wen Qing the one dismissed is a real referent error.

In the sixteenth year, together with Minister Tang Jinzhao he went to Shaanxi and Sichuan to investigate and impeach Governor Yang Mingyang and Provincial Administration Commissioner Li Yiwen; both were referred to strict deliberation. Soon after, upon reinvestigating the matter of Yang Mingyang being denounced, Wen Qing was stripped of his post.

In the sixteenth year, together with Minister Tang Jinzhao he went to Shaanxi and Sichuan to investigate and impeach Governor Yang Mingyang and Provincial Administration Commissioner Li Yiwen; both were referred to strict deliberation. Soon after, upon reinvestigating the matter of Yang Mingyang being denounced, Yang was stripped of his post.
Same referent error as r0001: 其職 after 按名颺被訐事 refers to Yang Mingyang, not Wen Qing; the literal English must demote Yang.
In the eighth month, as the enemy pressed harder, the court fled in haste; Wen Xiang was left as acting chief of the metropolitan gendarmerie to hold Beijing.
In the eighth month, as the enemy pressed harder, the court fled in haste; Wen Xiang was ordered to act as chief of the metropolitan gendarmerie and oversee those remaining in the capital.
Chinese 命…司留守 orders Wen Xiang to act as metropolitan gendarmerie chief and oversee those left behind; the idiomatic invents Beijing and weakens 命.
In the tenth month, after peace was concluded, he urged the court to return to Beijing so as to steady public morale.
In the tenth month, after peace was concluded, he urged the court to return so as to steady public morale.
回鑾 means the imperial return and does not name Beijing; the idiomatic English invents that place-name.
In the tenth month, on the return to Beijing, he joined the princes and ministers in asking that the two empress dowagers rule from behind the curtain.
In the tenth month, on the return of the court, he joined the princes and ministers in asking that the two empress dowagers rule from behind the curtain.
回鑾 again does not name Beijing; replacing “return to Beijing” with “return of the court” removes invented place detail.
In the eleventh year he was made grand secretary of the Titren Pavilion.
In the eleventh year he was made grand secretary of the Tiren Pavilion.
體仁閣 is Tiren Pavilion; Titren is a clear misspelling in the idiomatic English.
Wen Xiang stood sternly at court, sternly feared at home and abroad; the court situation relied on him to be maintained and did not change suddenly.
Wen Xiang stood sternly at court and was held in awe at home and abroad; the court situation relied on him to be maintained and did not change suddenly.
Duplicated “sternly” / “sternly feared” is unnatural English that obscures 為中外所嚴憚 as being held in awe; the proposed wording fixes a real translation defect.
and though spies were suborned, public outrage was united. On that basis the court was able to accept restraint and secure the present peace.
and though spies were suborned, public outrage was united. On that basis the foreigners could be held in restraint and the present peace settlement was formed.
得受羈縻 takes the foreigners as the restrained party by which the peace was formed; the idiomatic reverses agent and patient by making the court accept restraint.

A warm edict granted condolences, praising him as "upright in conduct, meticulous in statecraft, loyal and pure, bright and straightforward, sincere and fair—a pillar of the realm." He was posthumously made Grand Tutor, granted a hereditary Captain of Cavalry, inducted into the Shrine of Worthies, given three thousand taels for the funeral, and libations were offered by Prince Zaicheng. He received the posthumous title Wenhong, was buried in Mukden, and General Chong Shi was sent to perform the sacrifice.

A warm edict granted condolences, praising him as "upright in conduct, meticulous in statecraft, loyal and pure, bright and straightforward, sincere and fair—a pillar of the realm." He was posthumously made Grand Tutor, granted a hereditary Captain of Cavalry, inducted into the Shrine of Worthies, given three thousand taels for the funeral, and libations were offered by Prince Zaicheng. He received the posthumous title Wenzhong, was buried in Mukden, and General Chong Shi was sent to perform the sacrifice.
Posthumous name 文忠 is Wenzhong, not Wenhong; the idiomatic English mistransliterates the established reading.

A warm edict granted condolence gifts, praising him as "upright in personal conduct, meticulous in planning for the state, loyal and pure, bright and straight, sincere and earnest, fair and clear—a minister who is the state's sinews and heart," posthumously appointing him Grand Tutor, granting hereditary Captaincy of Cavalry, induction into the Shrine of Worthies, three thousand taels of silver for the funeral, dispatch of Prince Zaicheng to offer libations, posthumous title Wenhong, burial in Mukden, and ordering General Chong Shi to go and confer sacrifice.

A warm edict granted condolence gifts, praising him as "upright in personal conduct, meticulous in planning for the state, loyal and pure, bright and straight, sincere and earnest, fair and clear—a minister who is the state's sinews and heart," posthumously appointing him Grand Tutor, granting hereditary Captaincy of Cavalry, induction into the Shrine of Worthies, three thousand taels of silver for the funeral, dispatch of Prince Zaicheng to offer libations, posthumous title Wenzhong, burial in Mukden, and ordering General Chong Shi to go and confer sacrifice.
Posthumous name 文忠 is Wenzhong, not Wenhong; the literal English repeats the same mistransliteration.
In the fifteenth year, when the Empress Dowager resumed power, she recalled his earlier service and granted one altar of sacrifice.
In the fifteenth year, when the Empress Dowager returned power, she recalled his earlier service and granted one altar of sacrifice.
歸政 means the Empress Dowager returned governmental power to the emperor, not that she resumed power; the idiomatic English reverses the act.
He was promoted to grand secretary of the Grand Secretariat.
He was promoted to Academician of the Grand Secretariat.
內閣學士 is Cabinet Academician/Secretary, not 大學士 (Grand Secretary); the idiomatic English conflates the two ranks.
He was promoted to Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat.
He was promoted to Academician of the Grand Secretariat.
Same mistranslation of 內閣學士 as Grand Secretary in the literal field; Academician is the correct rank.
He was thrice transferred to reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
He was promoted through three transfers, reaching reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
三遷侍讀學士 means three successive promotions culminating in that office, not three transfers into the same post; the literal English misreads the formula.
